title: Kshamavani, the Jain day
hookLine: at the end of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of all beings: micchami dukkadam

cards: The same two words arrive from all over in one morning: a coworker's message, a cousin's post, a card from a neighbor. Micchami dukkadam.
No context, no list of what went wrong, just the phrase, sent to people near and far. For Jains, it marks the day at the end of Paryushana, a season of fasting, study and self-examination.

Jains call the closing day by more than one name; one of them is Kshamavani, the day of forgiveness. And the forgiveness asked for on that day doesn't stop at friends and family. It reaches every living thing.

teach.h: LET MY WRONG BE IN VAIN.
teach.b: First, the phrase. Micchami dukkadam comes from Prakrit, the old language of the Jain scriptures. Jains explain it as asking that whatever wrong I did be in vain, undone, without fruit.
It's a request, not a speech; nobody has to name what happened. Second, the verse behind it. Jains recite a short verse in their rite of repentance, called pratikramana.
In paraphrase: I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all, and enmity with none. It goes both ways in one breath: I forgive, and forgive me.

In Jain teaching, all living beings means exactly that: not only people, but animals, insects, the smallest creatures, the ones harmed without anyone noticing. That fits ahimsa, the Jain teaching of doing no harm.

So the asking reaches a whole world someone has moved through all year, often carelessly. Fourth, why strangers too. The message goes out to people you may not have wronged at all, or don't remember wronging.

teach.h: IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT.
teach.b: It doesn't wait for a complaint.
It assumes that in a year of living, a person steps on more toes than they know, and it clears the ground anyway: two words, sent wide, asking to start the next season clean.

how: At the close of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of family, friends, neighbors and all living beings, in person, by letter or by message, with the words micchami dukkadam; the pratikramana rite includes a verse forgiving and asking forgiveness of all beings.

o: the Jain day of forgiveness that closes Paryushana
a Hindu festival of lamps held in the autumn
the Jain fast that opens the season of study

games.q: the Jain day of forgiveness — tap the pairs.
p: a season of fasting and study
may my wrong be in vain

s: on this day Jains ask forgiveness only of people they know they've wronged
the asking goes wide, to all living beings, including those wronged without knowing.
the Jain verse both forgives and asks forgiveness
I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me.
micchami dukkadam requires naming the wrong
it's a request that the wrong be in vain; nobody has to name what happened.

games.q: it's the end of Paryushana. you can't think of anything you did to your neighbor this year. do you send micchami dukkadam anyway?
o: no: there's nothing to apologize for.
yes: the asking doesn't wait for a complaint.
only if they send it first.
games.why: the day assumes a year of living harms more than we notice, so the asking goes out wide, to known and unknown alike.

practice: Start close, and hold in mind for a few breaths one person you know you've hurt this year.

Then widen to people you may have hurt without knowing, a short reply, a missed call, someone you talked over, and wider still, to the creatures whose homes your life touches, until the circle is bigger than you can see.
If it fits for you, silently offer the Jain phrase, micchami dukkadam, to the whole circle, or, if you pray, do this in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Kshamavani. The Jain day of forgiveness at the close of Paryushana, when people ask pardon of all living beings. Today's word.

orig.note: Prakrit, the language of the Jain scriptures, written here in Devanagari.

carryVoice: Your line: micchami dukkadam. No list needed, and no one left out. Day nine hundred ninety-four, done.
